title: Mysuru Dasara & Jambu Savari
recognitionOrEra: Official State Festival (Nada Habba) · 10-Day Annual Observance
summary: Karnataka's state festival centered at Amba Vilas Palace, uniting royal processional heritage with regional folk ensembles during the Jambu Savari.
description: Recognized by the Government of Karnataka as Nada Habba (State Festival), Mysuru Dasara celebrates ten days of cultural performances, illuminated palace architecture, and the concluding Vijayadashami Jambu Savari procession. Folk troupes from across Karnataka—including Dollu Kunitha, Yakshagana, Veeragase, and Kamsale—march alongside cultural tableaus organized under the Department of Kannada and Culture.
verifiedFacts: Hosted annually around the illuminated Amba Vilas (Mysore Palace) complex in Mysuru.
The concluding Jambu Savari procession officially showcases state-recognized folk art troupes including Dollu Kunitha, Veeragase, and Kamsale.
Rooted in Wadiyar royal commemorations since Raja Wadiyar I (1610 CE) and Vijayanagara Mahanavami traditions.
preservationNote: State festival patronage provides annual performance commissions and travel support for rural folk art troupes across Karnataka.

title: Mysore Traditional Paintings
recognitionOrEra: GI Application No. 32 · Registered January 2006 (Certificate No. 26)
summary: Classical South Indian painting tradition noted for fine linework, muted mineral pigments, and raised zinc-oxide gesso relief gilded with 24-karat gold leaf.
description: Tracing its lineage to the Vijayanagara school and flourishing under Wadiyar royal patronage in Mysuru, Mysore traditional painting is distinguished by delicate brushwork and low-relief gesso work (prepared from zinc oxide and gum Arabic) embellished with pure gold foil (Swarna Patra). The craft received official Geographical Indication status in January 2006.
verifiedFacts: Geographical Indication Application No. 32 was registered in January 2006 under Certificate No. 26.
Raised ornamentation uses a traditional gesso paste compounded from zinc oxide and gum Arabic.
Surface gilding employs 24-karat gold leaf (Swarna Patra) paired with muted natural mineral tones.
preservationNote: GI certification protects authentic hand-gilded gesso technique and natural pigment standards against synthetic machine prints.

title: Yakshagana Dance-Drama
recognitionOrEra: Sangeet Natak Akademi Recognized Traditional Theatre
summary: Classical all-night coastal Karnataka theatre uniting sung poetic narratives, extempore dialogue, rhythmic percussion, and ornate wooden kirita crowns.
description: Practiced extensively across Udupi and Dakshina Kannada as well as Malnad districts, Yakshagana integrates live vocal narration by the Bhagavata, driving percussion from chande and maddale drums, vigorous footwork, and elaborated makeup with carved wooden crowns (kirita). Both Tenkuthittu and Badaguthittu coastal styles are documented by the Sangeet Natak Akademi.
verifiedFacts: Explicitly documented and awarded by the Sangeet Natak Akademi under India's national inventory of traditional performing arts.
Supported regionally by the Karnataka Sangeeta Nataka Academy and Karnataka Yakshagana Academy.
Performances combine improvised Kannada or Tulu prose dialogue with traditional poetic prasanga texts.
preservationNote: Academic fellowships and archival recordings safeguard elder Bhagavata vocal repertoires and traditional wooden headgear carving.

title: Dollu Kunitha
recognitionOrEra: Karnataka Janapada Academy Documented Folk Tradition
summary: High-energy ritual drum dance performed with large cylindrical dollu drums slung over the shoulder, featuring synchronized geometric formations.
description: Dollu Kunitha is a celebrated Karnataka folk percussion and dance form traditionally performed by artists associated with the Kuruba community and patronized by the Karnataka Janapada Academy. Performers beat heavy hollow drums while executing vigorous circular and half-circle formations, frequently featured in state cultural showcases including the Mysuru Dasara Jambu Savari.
verifiedFacts: Documented and patronized by the Karnataka Janapada Academy alongside certified regional folk troupes.
Performers carry hollow cylindrical drums (dollu) strapped over the shoulder and play synchronized rhythmic patterns.
Officially included in the Government of Karnataka's Mysuru Dasara Jambu Savari cultural procession.
preservationNote: Academy artist registries and festival stipends help transmit complex drum rhythms and troupe choreography to younger generations.

title: Group of Monuments at Hampi
recognitionOrEra: UNESCO World Heritage Site Ref. 241 · Inscribed 1986
summary: 14th to 16th century CE capital of the Vijayanagara Empire along the Tungabhadra River, famed for the Vittala stone chariot, Virupaksha temple, and royal aqueducts.
description: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1986 (Reference 241) under cultural criteria (i), (iii), and (iv), the Group of Monuments at Hampi spans 4,187.24 hectares of boulder-strewn river valley in Vijayanagara district. It preserves Dravidian temple complexes, monolithic carvings, fortified enclosures, and medieval urban water infrastructure.
verifiedFacts: Inscribed by UNESCO in 1986 at the 10th Session of the World Heritage Committee under Reference No. 241.
Covers a core property area of 4,187.24 hectares with a 19,453.62-hectare buffer zone.
Flourished between the 14th and 16th centuries CE as the imperial capital of Vijayanagara.
preservationNote: Protected by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) and Hampi World Heritage Area Management Authority; removed from the In Danger list in 2006.

title: Chennakesava Temple, Belur (Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas)
recognitionOrEra: UNESCO World Heritage Site Ref. 1670 · Inscribed September 18, 2023
summary: 12th-century Hoysala chloritic schist sanctuary commissioned by King Vishnuvardhana, recognized globally for stellate geometry and signed sculptures.
description: Together with Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu and Keshava Temple at Somnathapura, the Chennakesava Temple at Belur forms the UNESCO World Heritage serial property 'Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas' (Reference 1670), inscribed on September 18, 2023. Its star-shaped plinth, lathe-turned stone pillars, and detailed friezes represent the pinnacle of Karnata-Dravida soapstone architecture.
verifiedFacts: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on September 18, 2023 at the 45th Session under Reference No. 1670.
Earliest of the three inscribed Hoysala temples, commissioned in 1117 CE under King Vishnuvardhana.
Recognized under UNESCO criteria (i), (ii), and (iv) for stellate architecture and hyper-realistic soapstone carving.
preservationNote: Managed under Archaeological Survey of India conservation protocols tailored specifically for porous chloritic schist soapstone.
altText: Chennakesava Temple in Belur showing stellate platform and carved soapstone walls.

title: Badami Rock-Cut Cave Temples
recognitionOrEra: Early Chalukya Period (6th–8th Century CE · 578 CE Inscription)
summary: Four rock-cut sandstone cave shrines excavated into red cliffs overlooking Agastya Lake, marking the formative synthesis of Deccan temple design.
description: Hewn directly into rust-red sandstone escarpments at Vatapi (modern Badami), the four cave temples showcase Early Chalukyan sculptural and architectural experimentation. Cave 3 preserves an important dated inscription from 578 CE under ruler Mangalesha alongside monumental reliefs overlooking the Agastya water tank.
verifiedFacts: Cave 3 bears a dated 578 CE inscription attributed to Early Chalukya ruler Mangalesha.
Excavated into red sandstone cliffs flanking Agastya Lake in Bagalkot district.
Protected as a Monument of National Importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: Ongoing ASI monitoring tracks sandstone seepage and protects faint traces of original mineral ceiling pigments.

title: Dharwad Peda
summary: Caramelized, slightly grainy milk confection dusted in fine sugar powder, holding a culinary lineage exceeding 175 years in Line Bazar, Dharwad.
description: Originating over 175 years ago when the Thakur family migrated from Unnao to Dharwad, Dharwad Peda owes its characteristic deep brown hue and caramelized flavor to the prolonged slow boiling and continuous stirring of milk. Awarded Geographical Indication Registration No. 80 on September 9, 2008, it remains one of northern Karnataka's signature culinary heritage foods.
verifiedFacts: Registered under Geographical Indication Application No. 80 (certificate issued September 9, 2008).
Registered applicant is the Thakur's Dharwad Pedha Manufacturers' Welfare Trust in Line Bazar, Dharwad.
Characterized by slow-caramelized milk solids and a coating of fine sugar powder.
preservationNote: GI registration preserves traditional batch slow-reduction preparation and authentic regional dairy sourcing.

title: Mysore Silk
summary: Pure mulberry silk woven in Mysuru with authentic gold-and-silver zari borders, rooted in royal Wadiyar sericulture patronage since 1912.
description: Established by Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar in 1912 with Swiss looms to supply royal ceremonial attire, Mysore Silk is celebrated for its luminous drape, minimalist body, and rich pure-zari kasavu borders. Produced by Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation (KSIC) in Mysuru, it holds Geographical Indication Registration No. 22.
verifiedFacts: Awarded Geographical Indication Application No. 22 in 2005 to Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation (KSIC).
Woven exclusively from 100% pure mulberry silk and gold-dipped silver zari thread.
Factory established in Mysuru in 1912 under Maharaja Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar.
preservationNote: KSIC embeds unique numbered weave codes in every GI-certified saree to protect weavers from synthetic imitations.

title: Channapatna Toys & Dolls
summary: Ivory-wood (Aale Mara) turned wooden toys finished with natural vegetable pigments and glossy lac resin in Ramanagara district.
description: Known across Karnataka as 'Gombegala Ooru' (Toy Town), Channapatna produces smooth hand-turned wooden figures, puzzles, and dolls from seasoned Wrightia tinctoria (Aale Mara) timber. Artisans apply non-toxic botanical dyes mixed with shellac while the wood spins on lathes, earning GI status under Application No. 23.
verifiedFacts: Registered under Geographical Indication Application No. 23 in 2006.
Craft lineage traces back to 18th-century royal encouragement under Tipu Sultan and subsequent Mysuru guild patronage.
Uses seasoned Wrightia tinctoria wood colored with turmeric, indigo, kumkum, and lac.
preservationNote: Sustainable Aale Mara agroforestry and GI cooperative branding support artisan livelihoods in Ramanagara.

title: Bidriware Silver-Inlay Craft
summary: Distinctive matte-black zinc-copper alloy vessels and plaques inlaid with fine pure silver wire and oxidized using soil from Bidar Fort.
description: Originating in 14th–15th century Bahmani Bidar, Bidriware fuses Persian geometric and floral motifs with Deccan metallurgy. Artisans cast a blackened alloy of zinc and copper, engrave delicate grooves, hammer pure silver wire (tarkashi) or sheet (tah-nishan) flush into the surface, and oxidize the alloy to velvety black with nitrate-rich soil gathered from Bidar Fort.
verifiedFacts: Protected under Geographical Indication Application No. 21 (registered in 2006).
Matte black patina is chemically achieved using ammonium-nitrate-rich soil traditionally sourced from Bidar Fort.
Inlay work uses 99.9% pure silver wire or sheet hammered into hand-engraved alloy castings.
preservationNote: Bidar artisan cooperatives maintain hand-engraving and soil-oxidation apprenticeships under GI protection.

title: Kodagu Devarakadu (Sacred Forest Groves)
recognitionOrEra: Community Biocultural Heritage · Karnataka Forest Dept.
summary: Over 1,200 ancestral forest patches shielded across Kodagu through customary taboos against timber extraction, protecting endemic Western Ghats flora and springs.
description: Across the Western Ghats slopes of Kodagu, village communities and Kodava okkas have preserved sacred forest groves dedicated to village deities (Devarakadus) for centuries. Protected by unwritten customary law against logging or hunting, these groves safeguard old-growth biodiversity and perennial headwater springs feeding the Kaveri basin.
verifiedFacts: Kodagu preserves more than 1,200 documented Devarakadu sacred groves recognized by the Karnataka Forest Department.
Groves serve simultaneously as open-air forest shrines and community-protected watershed sanctuaries.
Co-stewarded by village temple committees alongside Karnataka Forest Department biodiversity surveys.
preservationNote: Joint Forest Management and boundary demarcation protect Devarakadus from agricultural encroachment.

title: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal
recognitionOrEra: UNESCO World Heritage Site Ref. 239 · Inscribed 1987
summary: Eighth-century Early Chalukyan coronation complex blending North Indian Nagara and South Indian Dravida temple spires along the Malaprabha River.
description: Inscribed by UNESCO in 1987 (Reference 239), Pattadakal—known anciently as Kisuvolal—was the ceremonial coronation city of the Chalukyas of Badami. Within one sandstone enclosure stand nine Hindu temples and a Jain sanctuary, led by the 8th-century Virupaksha Temple commissioned by Queen Lokamahadevi.
verifiedFacts: Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 under Reference No. 239.
Virupaksha Temple (c. 740 CE) was commissioned by Queen Lokamahadevi to commemorate Vikramaditya II's victory over the Pallavas.
Illustrates side-by-side experimentation in Dravida (Virupaksha, Mallikarjuna) and Nagara (Papanatha, Galaganatha) superstructures.
preservationNote: Conserved by the Archaeological Survey of India as a fenced national archaeological park along the Malaprabha.
altText: Virupaksha Temple and adjacent Chalukyan sandstone shrines at Pattadakal in Bagalkot district.

title: Aihole Temple Complex & Durga Temple
summary: Apsidal sandstone Durga Temple and over 120 Chalukyan shrines at Aihole, famed for the 634 CE Meguti Prashasti inscription of Ravikirti.
description: Often described by architectural historians as a cradle of Indian temple experimentation, Aihole (Aryapura) preserves over 120 temples from the Early Chalukyan period. Its standout Durga Temple (7th–8th century CE) features a rare apsidal Buddhist-chaitya plan wrapped in a colonnaded ambulatory corridor.
verifiedFacts: Meguti Jain Temple at Aihole preserves the 634 CE Sanskrit inscription composed by court poet Ravikirti under Pulakeshin II.
Durga Temple derives its name from 'durg' (fortress enclosure) and showcases an apsidal stone colonnade.
Protected and interpreted alongside an ASI site museum in Bagalkot district.
preservationNote: ASI conservation teams maintain sandstone plinths and manage visitor walkways across dispersed village monuments.
altText: Apsidal colonnaded Durga Temple at Aihole in Bagalkot district.

title: Ilkal Handloom Sarees
summary: Traditional northern Karnataka cotton-silk sarees distinguished by the unique 'tope-tenni' loop-joined crimson silk pallu and Kasuti motifs.
description: Woven in Ilkal town of Bagalkot district since at least the 8th century CE according to local weaving records, Ilkal sarees are celebrated for joining the cotton-warp body to a rich crimson or maroon silk pallu using three shuttles and a hand-twisted 'tope-tenni' loop technique.
verifiedFacts: Protected under Geographical Indication Application No. 76 (registered 2007).
Traditional borders feature characteristic Chikki Paras, Gomi, and Gaadi designs.
Uses three shuttles simultaneously for solid-colored borders alongside cotton-silk body weaves.
preservationNote: Handloom weaver societies in Ilkal uphold manual pit-loom weaving and natural-cotton warp preparation.

title: Pattadakal Dance Festival (Chalukya Utsava)
recognitionOrEra: Annual State Heritage Dance Festival · Government of Karnataka
summary: Classical music and dance festival staged against the illuminated 8th-century sandstone temples of Pattadakal, Badami, and Aihole.
description: Organized by the Government of Karnataka, Chalukya Utsava gathers classical Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, Kathak, and Hindustani performers onto open-air stages framed by Early Chalukyan temples at Pattadakal and Badami, honoring the artistic patronage of the 6th–8th century Badami Chalukyas.
verifiedFacts: Hosted annually across the Chalukyan triad of Pattadakal, Badami, and Aihole.
Showcases classical Indian dance forms and northern Karnataka folk ensembles.
Promoted jointly by KSTDC and the Karnataka Department of Kannada and Culture.
preservationNote: Open-air stage placement is regulated outside sensitive ASI stone temple plinths.

title: Ballari Fort (Upper & Lower Citadels)
summary: Two-level granite fortification crowning Bellary Gudda monolith, originally built by Hanumappa Nayaka and expanded in dressed stone under Hyder Ali.
description: Rising dramatically above Ballari city on a massive granite dome (Ballari Gudda), Ballari Fort consists of an Upper Fort on the summit attributed to Hande Hanumappa Nayaka of the Vijayanagara period and an 18th-century Lower Fort fortified with deep moats and stone bastions under Hyder Ali.
verifiedFacts: Features rainwater-harvesting granite rock cisterns engineered inside the upper summit citadel.
Lower Fort walls and barracks date to 18th-century Mysore Sultanate and subsequent garrison phases.
Declared a Monument of National Importance under the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: ASI preserves perimeter ramparts while local heritage groups advocate trail signage and summit tank cleaning.
altText: Upper stone ramparts of Ballari Fort atop the granite hill in Ballari district.

title: Sandur Lambani Embroidery
summary: Vibrant geometric needlework combining 14 traditional stitches, natural darning, cowrie shells, and tiny mirrors crafted by Lambani women artisans in Sandur.
description: Practiced by Lambani (Banjara) women around Sandur in Ballari district, Sandur Lambani embroidery layers colorful cotton threads—in up to 14 distinct hand stitches such as kilan, vele, and bakiya—with small mirrors (shisha) and beads over handloom khadi or cotton textiles.
verifiedFacts: Awarded Geographical Indication Application No. 132 in 2010.
Revived and organized through the Sandur Kushala Kala Kendra (SKKK) women's cooperative.
Incorporates geometric patchwork (khilan) and mirror-work rooted in pastoral Banjara dress traditions.
preservationNote: Cooperative fair-trade sales sustain hundreds of women embroiderers across Sandur taluk villages.
altText: Traditional Lambani embroidered textile featuring vivid geometric stitching and mirror accents.

title: Ballari Doddata & Bayalata Folk Theatre
summary: Open-air nocturnal folk dance-drama tradition of the eastern Deccan plains blending heroic mythological songs, maddale drums, and circular choreography.
description: Performed in village squares across Ballari and neighboring North Karnataka districts after harvest, Doddata ('Big Play') is an open-air musical drama accompanied by harmonium, maddale, and cymbals, celebrating classical epics and regional Ballari legends.
verifiedFacts: Documented by the Karnataka Bayalata Academy and Karnataka Janapada Academy.
Performances unfold overnight on raised village platforms (bayalu means open ground).
Distinct from coastal Yakshagana in its northern Kannada poetic meters and harmonium-maddale accompaniment.
preservationNote: Academy grants and annual folk theatre festivals preserve handwritten bayalata scripts and troupe costumes.

title: Belagavi Fort & Kamala Basadi
recognitionOrEra: Ratta Dynasty (1204 CE) & Adil Shahi Eras
summary: Oval stone-and-moat fortress enclosing the 1204 CE Chalukyan-style Kamala Basadi Jain temple, famous for its inverted stone lotus ceiling.
description: Originally built in stone around 1204 CE by Bichiraja under Ratta king Kartavirya IV, Belagavi Fort preserves a rare juxtaposition of periods: the intricately carved Kamala Basadi (whose ceiling displays a 72-petal stone lotus), the 16th-century Safa Masjid, and layered defensive bastions.
verifiedFacts: Kamala Basadi inside the fort dates to 1204 CE under Ratta ruler Kartavirya IV.
Houses a black-stone idol of Neminatha Tirthankara beneath a carved lotus dome.
Later reinforced with wide outer moats and arched gateways during Adil Shahi rule.
preservationNote: Protected by Karnataka State Department of Archaeology and Belagavi Cantonment heritage stewards.
altText: Jain temple and carved stone facade inside Belagavi Fort in Belagavi district.

title: Kittur Fort & Kittur Utsav
recognitionOrEra: 1824 CE Anti-Colonial Heritage · Annual State Festival
summary: Historic fort and annual state festival commemorating Rani Chennamma of Kittur's 1824 armed defiance against the British East India Company.
description: Each October, Kittur Utsav gathers performers, historians, and citizens at Kittur Fort in Belagavi district to honor Rani Chennamma (1778–1829) and her lieutenant Sangolli Rayanna, whose 1824 defense of Kittur's sovereignty predated the 1857 uprising by more than three decades.
verifiedFacts: In October 1824, Rani Chennamma's forces defeated an initial British expedition led by St. John Thackeray at Kittur Fort.
An archaeological museum beside the fort ruins preserves Desi dynasty stone sculptures, weapons, and inscriptions.
Kittur Utsav is officially celebrated annually by the Government of Karnataka.
preservationNote: The Kittur Development Authority maintains the fort ruins, Rani Chennamma Memorial, and Sangolli Rayanna heritage circuit.
altText: Kittur Fort grounds and memorial gateway in Belagavi district, Karnataka.

title: Belagavi Kunda
summary: Rich, caramelized, soft-granulated milk fudge simmered slowly with sugar and cardamom in Belagavi's traditional sweet shops.
description: Belagavi Kunda is a signature northern Karnataka milk-based confection crafted by simmering fresh buffalo or cow milk for hours until its natural lactose caramelizes into a warm amber-brown, mildly grainy khoya mass scented with green cardamom.
verifiedFacts: Prepared through slow open-pan reduction of whole milk with sugar rather than artificial colorings.
Widely associated with family-run sweet establishments across Belagavi city for over a century.
Closely tied to Belagavi's festive hospitality alongside Mandige.
preservationNote: Traditional wood- and gas-simmered copper-and-iron kadai batches remain prized over mass industrial variants.
altText: Caramelized Belagavi Kunda milk sweet garnished with nuts.

title: Devanahalli Fort
recognitionOrEra: 1501 CE Avati Nadaprabhu & Mysore Eras · ASI
summary: Oval stone-walled fort built around 1501 CE by Malla Byregowda and strengthened in granite by Hyder Ali, enclosing ancient Venugopalaswamy shrines.
description: Constructed originally in mud around 1501 CE by Malla Byregowda of the Avati chieftains, Devanahalli Fort was later rebuilt in dressed granite with 12 circular bastions under Hyder Ali. Inside its ramparts stand the Vijayanagara-period Venugopalaswamy Temple and Siddheshwara Temple.
verifiedFacts: Original mud fortification dates to c. 1501 CE under Malla Byregowda of the Avati Nadaprabhu lineage.
Encircled by twelve semicircular bastions with gun embrasures and decorated temple pillars inside.
Protected as a Monument of National Importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: ASI oversees stone bastion restoration and protects the inner Venugopalaswamy temple carvings.
altText: Granite bastions and entrance wall of Devanahalli Fort in Bengaluru Rural district.

title: Ghati Subramanya Brahmotsava & Cattle Fair
recognitionOrEra: Annual Makara Pushya Temple & Agrarian Fair
summary: Centuries-old hilltop temple festival and Hallikar cattle fair near Doddaballapura uniting rural agrarian heritage with sacred worship.
description: Every Pushya Shuddha Shashti, Ghati Subramanya near Doddaballapura hosts both its temple Brahmotsava and one of southern Karnataka's most famous traditional cattle fairs, celebrating native Hallikar draught breeds alongside folk ensembles.
verifiedFacts: Unique shrine housing a single stone idol combining Lord Subramanya (front) and Narasimha (back).
Annual Pushya Shashti fair attracts farming households showcasing prized Hallikar cattle.
Celebrated with traditional chariot processions and rural folk percussion.
preservationNote: Recognized by Karnataka agrarian heritage advocates as vital for preserving indigenous Hallikar cattle lineages.
altText: Ghati Subramanya Brahmotsava and Cattle Fair in Bengaluru Rural

title: Doddaballapura Silk & Saree Weaving
recognitionOrEra: Historic Silk Weaving Cluster · Bengaluru Rural
summary: Long-standing silk and cotton-silk saree weaving cluster north of Bengaluru known for zari borders and jacquard brocade patterns.
description: Doddaballapura has functioned for generations as one of Karnataka's largest weaving centers, producing pure silk and cotton-silk sarees whose dyed warps and jacquard borders support thousands of weaver households.
verifiedFacts: Historically supplied regional markets across Old Mysore with pure silk and festive sarees.
Features specialized warp-sizing, dyeing, and dobby/jacquard border craftsmanship.
Recognized under Karnataka Handloom and Textile Development cluster programs.
preservationNote: State cooperative yarn banks help traditional pit- and frame-loom weavers manage silk input costs.

title: Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace & Bangalore Fort
summary: Two-storey carved teakwood summer pavilion adorned with floral frescoes beside the stone Delhi Gate of 18th-century Bangalore Fort.
description: Begun by Hyder Ali in 1781 and completed by Tipu Sultan in 1791 CE as 'Rashk-e-Jannat' (Envy of Heaven), this Indo-Islamic pavilion stands entirely on fluted teakwood pillars crowned by lotus brackets and painted with vegetable-dye floral motifs.
verifiedFacts: Completed in 1791 CE using teakwood columns, cusped arches, and ornate balconies.
Stands adjacent to the surviving stone bastion and Kote Venkataramana Temple inside Old Fort.
Maintained with a historical gallery by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI).
preservationNote: ASI conducts periodic conservation of the original vegetable-pigment teakwood frescoes and stone battlements.

title: Bangalore Palace
summary: Tudor-Revival and Scottish Gothic palace built for Maharaja Chamarajendra Wadiyar X, featuring turreted battlements, stained glass, and carved wood interiors.
description: Constructed in 1887 CE on grounds purchased from Rev. John Garrett for Maharaja Chamarajendra Wadiyar X, Bangalore Palace blends Tudor-style granite battlements and vine-clad towers with South Indian carved teak ceilings, Raja Ravi Varma paintings, and royal durbar halls.
verifiedFacts: Completed in 1887 CE across 454 acres in Sadashivanagar / Jayamahal, Bengaluru.
Modeled in part after Windsor Castle with fortified towers, Gothic windows, and open courtyard.
Houses historic photographs, floral motifs, and royal furnishings of the Mysuru Wadiyars.
preservationNote: Preserved as a historic landmark and cultural venue in central Bengaluru.
altText: Tudor-style turrets and ivy-covered stone facade of Bangalore Palace in Bengaluru.

title: Bengaluru Karaga Shaktyotsava
recognitionOrEra: 300+ Year Old Civic Festival · Old Pete, Bengaluru
summary: All-night Chaitra full-moon procession led by the Thigala community, balancing an ornate floral jasmine pyramid (Karaga) from Dharmaraya Swamy Temple.
description: Celebrated on Chaitra Purnima around the historic Dharmaraya Swamy Temple in Bengaluru's Old Pete, Bengaluru Karaga is one of the city's oldest living festivals. The priest balances an earthen pot crowned with tall jasmine tiers—without touching it by hand—along a historic route visiting both Hindu shrines and Hazrat Tawakkal Mastan Dargah, symbolizing communal harmony.
verifiedFacts: Observed annually on Chaitra Purnima (March–April) starting at Dharmaraya Swamy Temple near Nagarathpete.
Procession traditionally pauses at the centuries-old Hazrat Tawakkal Mastan Dargah in Cottonpet.
Led by the Veerakumaras of the Thigala community upholding centuries-old ritual discipline.
preservationNote: Municipal authorities and temple trusts coordinate traffic-free old-city heritage corridors during the midnight procession.
altText: Traditional carrier balancing the floral Bengaluru Karaga crown during the annual festival.

title: Bisi Bele Bath
recognitionOrEra: Classic Old Mysore & Bengaluru Culinary Tradition
summary: Aromatic hot spiced rice, toor dal, tamarind, and vegetable dish infused with freshly roasted Byadgi-chilli masala and finished with ghee and boondi.
description: Originating in the royal kitchens of the Mysore Palace and popularized across Bengaluru's historic tiffin rooms and darshinis, Bisi Bele Bath ('hot lentil rice') balances tangy tamarind, nutty lentils, seasonal vegetables, and a signature roasted spice blend featuring Marathi moggu, cinnamon, and dry coconut.
verifiedFacts: Traced historically to 19th–20th century Mysore Palace culinary lineages before becoming a Bengaluru staple.
Distinctive spice blend includes byadgi chillies, coriander seeds, cinnamon, cloves, and kapok buds (marathi moggu).
Traditionally served piping hot with clarified butter (ghee) and crisp boondi or potato chips.
preservationNote: Maintained as a flagship dish in heritage Kannada households and traditional vegetarian eateries.
altText: Serving of traditional Karnataka Bisi Bele Bath garnished with crisp boondi.

title: Bidar Fort, Rangeen Mahal & Karez Aqueducts
recognitionOrEra: 15th-Century Bahmani Capital · ASI & World Monuments Fund
summary: Laterite plateau citadel built under Ahmad Shah Bahmani featuring polychrome Persian tiles, Tarkash Mahal, and a medieval subterranean karez water system.
description: Constructed atop a red laterite escarpment around 1428 CE when Ahmad Shah Wali moved the Bahmani capital from Kalaburagi, Bidar Fort encloses over 30 monuments including Rangeen Mahal—famous for its carved teakwood brackets and mother-of-pearl inlay—and the historic subterranean karez (qanat) water channels.
verifiedFacts: Surrounded by a triple-layered rock-cut moat carved directly into laterite bedrock.
Bidar's karez subterranean aqueduct system represents one of India's rare surviving Deccan qanat water networks.
Nearby Mahmud Gawan Madrasa (1472 CE) stands as an emblem of Bahmani scholarship and tilework.
preservationNote: Conserved jointly by ASI, Bidar Heritage Trust, and local community initiatives restoring the karez waterwells.
altText: Arched facade and laterite courtyard of Rangeen Mahal inside Bidar Fort.

title: Basavakalyan Vachana & Anubhava Mantapa Legacy
summary: Twelfth-century egalitarian poetic and spiritual tradition led by Basavanna, Akka Mahadevi, and Allama Prabhu at Kalyana (Basavakalyan).
description: During the 12th century CE in Kalyana (modern Basavakalyan, Bidar district), philosopher-statesman Basavanna and fellow Sharanas convened the Anubhava Mantapa—an open spiritual assembly welcoming poets from diverse castes and trades. Their Kannada prose-lyrics (Vachanas) remain foundational to Kannada literature and social equality.
verifiedFacts: Vachana poets included Basavanna, Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahadevi, Chennabasavanna, and Jedara Dasimayya.
Emphasized 'Kayaka' (dignity of labor) and 'Dasoha' (community sharing) in everyday vernacular Kannada.
Commemorated annually at Basavakalyan Fort and Anubhava Mantapa heritage complex.
preservationNote: Critical editions of thousands of palm-leaf Vachanas are preserved by Karnataka's universities and state academies.
altText: Basavakalyan 12th-Century Vachana Heritage in Bidar District

title: Biligirirangana Swamy Temple (BR Hills)
recognitionOrEra: Hilltop Dravidian Shrine · BRT Wildlife Corridor
summary: Ancient cliff-edge Dravidian temple perched atop the white-rock Biligiri hills at the confluence of the Eastern and Western Ghats.
description: Perched at an elevation of roughly 1,550 meters overlooking the Biligiriranganatha Swamy Temple (BRT) forests, this ancient hilltop sanctuary is revered equally by regional pilgrims and the indigenous Soliga community, featuring a towering Dravidian gopura and granite pillared courtyard.
verifiedFacts: Situated at the ecological junction linking the Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats.
Deeply woven into Soliga oral lore and annual community temple festivals.
Preserves Dravidian mandapa architecture overlooking dense shola and deciduous forests.
preservationNote: Pilgrim traffic and temple festivals are coordinated with BRT Tiger Reserve ecological guidelines.
altText: Biligirirangana Swamy Temple complex perched atop the forested BR Hills in Chamarajanagar district.

title: Male Mahadeshwara Hills Pilgrimage & Deepavali Jatra
summary: Major forest-hill pilgrimage honoring saint-miracle worker Sri Male Mahadeshwara, accompanied by traditional Kamsale performers and folk epics.
description: Set amidst forested hills in Hanur taluk, Sri Male Mahadeshwara Betta commemorates the 15th-century saint Mahadeshwara through vibrant Deepavali, Ugadi, and Maha Shivaratri fairs where devotees walk forest trails singing folk ballads accompanied by bronze kamsale cymbals.
verifiedFacts: Dedicated to Sri Male Mahadeshwara, revered across southern Karnataka and the Kaveri borderlands.
Devotees (Devara Guddaru) perform Beesu Kamsale rituals during annual temple fairs.
Connected historically to Manteswamy and Neelagara oral folk epic lineages.
preservationNote: Regional development boards maintain plastic-free hill-forest pilgrimage routes and traditional anna dasoha halls.
altText: Sri Male Mahadeshwara Swamy Temple complex nestled in the hills of Chamarajanagar district.

title: Beesu Kamsale Devotional Dance
summary: Acrobatic and devotional folk dance performed with resonant bronze cup-and-disc cymbals (kamsale) praising Sri Male Mahadeshwara.
description: Practiced across Chamarajanagar, Mysuru, and Mandya by devotees known as Devara Guddaru, Beesu Kamsale combines rhythmic hand-cymbal percussion with energetic circles, paired acrobatics, and sung narrative epics recounting the miracles of Male Mahadeshwara.
verifiedFacts: Named after the heavy brass-bronze cymbal pair (batalu and gari) struck in complex syncopated beats.
Recognized by the Karnataka Janapada Academy and featured regularly at Mysuru Dasara.
Deeply connected with oral folk literature (Janapada Mahakavya) of southern Karnataka.
preservationNote: Recorded by Karnataka Janapada Academy and folklorists across Chamarajanagar and Mysuru.
altText: Traditional Karnataka Beesu Kamsale folk artist performing with brass cymbals.

title: Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple Complex
recognitionOrEra: 9th–16th Century CE (Bana, Nolamba, Chola, Hoysala & Vijayanagara) · ASI
summary: Multi-dynastic granite sanctuary at the foot of Nandi Hills showcasing Bana-Nolamba reliefs, Chola inscriptions, and a majestic Vijayanagara stepped tank.
description: Located in Nandi village beneath Nandi Durga, Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple preserves over seven centuries of South Indian architectural evolution in one complex—from 9th-century Bana/Nolamba twin shrines and perforated stone windows to an expansive Vijayanagara kalyani tank.
verifiedFacts: Copperplate and stone inscriptions link its founding to 9th-century Bana Queen Ratnavali and Nolamba rulers.
Features twin central shrines—Arunachaleshwara and Bhoganandeeshwara—connected by a shared mandapa.
Protected as a Monument of National Importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: ASI maintains the carved black-basalt Navaranga pillars and stepped Shringi Tirtha tank.
altText: Panoramic courtyard view of the Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple complex in Chikkaballapura district.

title: Nandi Maha Shivaratri & Rathotsava
recognitionOrEra: Annual Maha Shivaratri Temple & Agrarian Fair
summary: Ten-day Brahmarathotsava and traditional Hallikar cattle fair held beneath Nandi Hills around the ancient Bhoga Nandeeshwara complex.
description: Coinciding with Maha Shivaratri, Nandi village transforms into a major religious and rural gathering where wooden temple chariots are drawn alongside exhibitions of prized indigenous Hallikar cattle and local folk music.
verifiedFacts: Centers around the 9th-century Bhoga Nandeeshwara and hilltop Yoga Nandeeshwara shrines.
Integrates traditional agrarian cattle trading with classical and folk musical performances.
Sustained by local village committees in Chikkaballapura taluk.
preservationNote: Heritage stewards regulate vehicle access near the historic temple tank during peak festival crowds.
altText: Nandi Maha Shivaratri Festival in Chikkaballapura

title: Amruteshwara Temple, Amruthapura
recognitionOrEra: 1196 CE Hoysala Period · ASI Protected Monument
summary: Ornate Hoysala soapstone temple erected in 1196 CE by general Amriteshwara Dandanayaka, renowned for scalloped dome ceilings and epic friezes.
description: Commissioned in 1196 CE under Hoysala king Veera Ballala II by minister-general Amriteshwara Dandanayaka, Amruteshwara Temple combines a large open mantapa with lathe-turned bell-shaped pillars, delicate deep-carved ceiling lotuses, and miniature wall reliefs of the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Bhagavata.
verifiedFacts: Built in 1196 CE during the reign of Hoysala emperor Veera Ballala II.
Outer enclosure wall preserves over a hundred circular carved lotus medallions and narrative panels.
Protected as a Monument of National Importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: ASI maintains the chloritic schist masonry and surrounding landscaped garden in Tarikere taluk.
altText: Amruteshwara Temple at Amruthapura in Chikkamagaluru district showing Hoysala soapstone facade.

title: Vidyashankara Temple & Sringeri Heritage
summary: Unique apsidal granite shrine on the Tunga River featuring twelve zodiac pillars aligned so sunrise illuminates each corresponding solar month.
description: Built in the mid-14th century CE in honor of pontiff Vidyatirtha at Sringeri Sharada Peetham, Vidyashankara Temple bridges late Hoysala stellate planning with early Vijayanagara granite carving. Its twelve massive zodiac (Rashi) pillars inside the central hall are engineered to receive morning sunlight sequentially across the solar calendar.
verifiedFacts: Stands on the bank of the Tunga River at Sringeri, seat of the first Matha founded by Adi Shankaracharya.
Twelve zodiac pillars (Rashi Stambhas) feature carved lions holding rotating stone balls in their mouths.
Protected under the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: Tunga riverbank flood barriers and heritage masonry maintenance safeguard the 14th-century plinth.
altText: Vidyashankara Temple at Sringeri surrounded by morning Malnad mist in Chikkamagaluru district.

title: Antike-Pantike Deepavali Folk Singing
recognitionOrEra: Living Malnad Agrarian Custom · Western Ghats
summary: Lantern-lit nocturnal harvest custom across Malnad villages where singing troupes carry sacred flame ('deepa') from house to house during Deepavali.
description: Unique to the Malnad uplands of Chikkamagaluru and Shivamogga, Antike-Pantike takes place over the nights of Deepavali. Carrying a lit oil torch or earthen lamp, villagers walk through misty coffee and arecanut estates singing traditional Kannada ballads and blessing each household's granary and cattle shed.
verifiedFacts: Documented by Kannada folklorists as a distinctive Western Ghats harvest-light ritual.
Songs invoke prosperity, monsoon balance, and community solidarity across neighboring estates.
Passed down orally across generations in Malnad farming villages.
preservationNote: Local cultural forums organize village-level gatherings to encourage younger residents to learn traditional melodies.
altText: Antike-Pantike Deepavali Torch-Singing Tradition in Chikkamagaluru

title: Chitradurga Fort (Yelu Suttina Kote)
summary: Seven concentric granite fortification walls embracing natural boulders, 19 gateways, stepwells, and the famous Obavvana Kindi crevice.
description: Expanded over three centuries by the Palegars (Nayakas) of Chitradurga—especially Madakari Nayaka V—Chitradurga Fort weaves seven defensive stone rings directly into granite hills, featuring interconnected rainwater reservoirs that ensured the garrison never ran dry during prolonged sieges.
verifiedFacts: Features seven concentric stone ramparts, 19 gateways, 38 postern gates, and monumental granaries.
Houses the narrow rock passage known as Obavvana Kindi, honoring Onake Obavva's defense against Hyder Ali's troops.
Protected as a Monument of National Importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: ASI maintains the historic stone reservoirs, Hidimbeshwara temple, and granite battlements.
altText: Granite ramparts and rocky hill fortification of Chitradurga Fort in Chitradurga district.

title: Molakalmuru Pure Silk Sarees
summary: Handwoven mulberry silk sarees from Molakalmuru famed for triple-shuttle interlocked borders, temple motifs, and richly contrasted pallus.
description: Woven in the northernmost taluk of Chitradurga district, Molakalmuru sarees use pure mulberry silk with traditional 'korvai' three-shuttle border interlocking, displaying lotus, rudraksha, elephant, and temple motifs along vibrant contrasting pallus.
verifiedFacts: Registered under Geographical Indication Application No. 53 in 2007.
Distinctive for hand-interlocked borders woven using three shuttles without mechanical jacquards in classic styles.
Supported by weaver guilds centered in Molakalmuru town.
preservationNote: GI certification and cooperative design training sustain traditional handloom weaving families in Chitradurga.

title: Kadri Manjunatha Temple & Bronze Lokeshwara
recognitionOrEra: 10th–11th Century CE (968 CE Dated Bronze) · Coastal Heritage
summary: Ancient coastal shrine on Kadri hills housing a rare dated 968 CE bronze statue of Lokeshwara commissioned by Alupa ruler Kundavarma.
description: Set beneath laterite hills with nine natural spring tanks (Kashi Bhageerathi Tirtha) in Mangaluru, Kadri Manjunatha Temple preserves one of South India's finest dated bronzes—a 968 CE multi-armed Lokeshwara image bearing a Sanskrit inscription of Alupa king Kundavarma—illustrating the coastal transition between Vajrayana and Natha Shaiva traditions.
verifiedFacts: Houses a dated 968 CE bronze Lokeshwara image cast by Alupa dynasty ruler Kundavarma.
Features coastal sloped tiled roofs adapted to intense Arabian Sea monsoon rainfall.
Adjacent to rock-cut caves on Kadri hill associated with Matsyendranatha and Gorakhnatha.
preservationNote: Conserved by temple trustees and Karnataka State archaeology documentation.
altText: Kadri Manjunatha Temple courtyard and coastal tiled roofs in Mangaluru, Dakshina Kannada.

title: Kambala (Seasonal Coastal Paddy-Field Tradition)
summary: Traditional winter water-buffalo sprint across parallel slushy paddy tracks held across Dakshina Kannada and Udupi to honor agrarian cycles.
description: Observed annually between November and March across coastal Tulunadu (Dakshina Kannada and Udupi), Kambala celebrates post-monsoon rice cultivation. Paired buffaloes guided by a barefoot runner race down parallel flooded tracks (kere) in categories such as Kane Halage, Negilu, and Hagga.
verifiedFacts: Rooted in centuries-old rural thanksgiving to Kadri Manjunatha and agricultural land spirits.
Categorized into traditional disciplines including Negilu (plough), Hagga (rope), Adda Halage, and Kane Halage.
Governed by modern animal-welfare and regulated racing rules enacted in Karnataka.
preservationNote: District Kambala committees enforce strict veterinary checks and non-cruelty regulations across coastal venues.
altText: Pair of buffaloes and runner racing down water-filled paddy tracks during Kambala in Tulunadu.

title: Bhoota Kola (Tuluva Daivaradhane)
recognitionOrEra: Living Tuluva Ancestral Ritual · Coastal Karnataka
summary: All-night community spirit-worship ritual uniting ornate palm-frond costumes, bell-metal anklets, Tulu Paddana epics, and village dispute resolution.
description: Deeply embedded in the social fabric of Dakshina Kannada and Udupi, Bhoota Kola (or Daiva Nema) honors guardian village spirits (Daivas) such as Panjurli, Guliga, and Koragajja. Ritual specialists don towering siras/mudi crowns of tender coconut fronds and brass anklets while villagers listen to sung Tulu Paddana histories.
verifiedFacts: Accompanied by oral Tulu Paddanas—narrative folk epics passed down across generations.
Functions historically as a village moral and agrarian justice forum uniting communities.
Documented by Tulu Sahitya Academy and Udupi Regional Resources Centre for Folk Performing Arts (RRC).
preservationNote: RRC Udupi and Tulu academies record endangered Paddana recitations and ritual craft lineages.
altText: Traditional Tuluva Bhoota Kola performer adorned in sacred crown and ceremonial attire.

title: Santhebennur Pushkarani & Vasant Mantapa
summary: Monumental stepped stone temple tank centered around an ornate octagonal Indo-Islamic-influenced Vasant Mantapa pavilion.
description: Constructed in the late 16th century CE by local chieftain Kenga Hanumappa Nayaka, the Santhebennur Pushkarani is an expansive square stepped tank flanked by eight minar-topped pavilions and a graceful octagonal central pavilion once used for spring water festivals.
verifiedFacts: Built by Kenga Hanumappa Nayaka of the Basavapatna/Santhebennur lineage in the 16th century CE.
Blends Vijayanagara stepped pushkarani stone geometry with Deccan cusped arches and corner minars.
Protected as a Monument of National Importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: ASI preserves the granite steps, central pavilion, and adjacent Musafirkhana courtyard.
altText: Stepped granite perimeter and octagonal central pavilion of Santhebennur Pushkarani in Davanagere.

title: Davanagere Benne Dose
summary: Golden, crisp-yet-fluffy fermented rice-and-poha crepes generously cooked on cast-iron griddles with fresh white butter, potato palya, and coconut chutney.
description: Created in Davanagere's bustling cotton-mill neighborhoods during the early 20th century, Davanagere Benne Dose is distinguished by puffed rice (mandakki/poha) in the batter and generous dollops of white churned butter melted over blazing griddles, served with mild mashed potato palya and watery spiced coconut chutney.
verifiedFacts: Batter combines rice, urad dal, and soaked puffed rice or flattened rice for a crisp exterior and airy interior.
Traditionally cooked on thick iron tavas with fresh white unsalted butter rather than oil.
Iconic culinary identity of Davanagere city across Karnataka.
preservationNote: Family-run eateries in Davanagere preserve original cast-iron griddle preparation and spice ratios.
altText: Davanagere Benne Dose Culinary Heritage

title: Chandramouleswara Temple, Unkal
summary: Cruciform black-stone Chalukyan temple featuring four ornate cardinal doorways, dual Nandi shrines, and carved dancing figure brackets.
description: Situated beside Unkal Lake between Hubballi and Dharwad, the 12th-century Chandramouleswara Temple exemplifies mature Kalyana Chalukyan design with symmetrical cruciform sanctum axes, finely turned black-chloritic schist pillars, and pierced stone jali lattice screens.
verifiedFacts: Dates to the 11th–12th century CE under the Western (Kalyana) Chalukyas.
Distinctive cruciform plan houses dual Nandi pavilions oriented along the east-west axis.
Protected as a Monument of National Importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.
preservationNote: Maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India Dharwad Circle.
altText: Carved sandstone facade of the 12th-century Chandramouleswara Temple at Unkal in Dharwad district.

title: Dharwad Kasuti Hand Embroidery
summary: Intricate counted-thread embroidery using four reversible stitches (Gavanti, Murgi, Negi, Menthi) depicting temple gopuras, chariots, and tulsi pots.
description: Dating back to Chalukyan-era textile needlework traditions across Dharwad and northern Karnataka, Kasuti ('kai' meaning hand and 'suti' meaning cotton thread) is executed strictly by counting warp and weft threads without tracing patterns, ensuring both sides of the fabric look identical.
verifiedFacts: Registered under Geographical Indication Application No. 55 in 2007.
Employs four traditional stitch families: Gavanti (double running), Murgi (zigzag), Negi (darning), and Menthi (cross-stitch).
Commonly embellishes Ilkal sarees, Guledgudda blouses, and festive garments.
preservationNote: Women's craft societies in Dharwad and Hubballi sustain traditional counted-thread embroidery workshops.
altText: Dharwad Kasuti Hand Embroidery Tradition

title: Dharwad Hindustani Classical Music Lineage
summary: Cultural renaissance that made Dharwad a national bastion of Kirana and Jaipur-Atrauli Hindustani vocal music, nurturing Bharat Ratna and Padma laureates.
description: Remarkably positioned in northern Karnataka where Carnatic and Marathi-Hindustani streams meet, Dharwad–Hubballi nourished some of India's towering Hindustani vocalists—including Sawai Gandharva, Mallikarjun Mansur, Gangubai Hangal, Basavaraj Rajguru, Kumar Gandharva, and Bharat Ratna Pandit Bhimsen Joshi.
verifiedFacts: Home to institutions such as the Gangubai Hangal Gurukul and Dr. Mallikarjun Mansur Memorial Museum.
Blended Kirana, Gwalior, and Jaipur-Atrauli gharana styles within Kannada-speaking sabhas.
Continues through annual memorial music festivals across Dharwad and Kundgol.
preservationNote: State memorials and archival audio collections preserve rare live recordings of Dharwad's classical maestros.
altText: Dharwad Hindustani Classical Music Lineage
